records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed Accident Analysis & Prevention article, available online by 22 May 2026 and assigned to volume 234 (September 2026), article 108592
records.decision_reason: Gemini is the sole primary thematic analyst of eight think-aloud transcripts, with quote-level source checking and an unscored cross-model robustness comparison but no independent human theme analysis.

Research objective.value: Identify experienced driving assessors' requirements for transitions of control in Automated Lane Keeping Systems during on-road Wizard-of-Oz use.
Research objective.anchor: human requirements during transitions of control

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: LLM-assisted thematic analysis of think-aloud protocols

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Eight usable on-road think-aloud recordings were locally transcribed with WhisperV3, cleaned and manually corrected; the complete transcripts were passed in one reproduced prompt to Gemini 3.0 Pro Preview to generate themes and select quotations. Authors checked selected quotations against recordings and repeated the prompt once with three alternative frontier models as a narrative robustness check.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: inductive within a prespecified transitions-of-control research question

Domain.value: automated driving and transitions of control

Number of participants.value: 10 professional driving assessors recruited; two excluded because of audio failure; analytic n=8 (six men, two women)

Approximate corpus size.value: mean experimental phase 72.6 minutes; 54 nonurgent take-over requests, 34 urgent requests, and 43 discretionary takeovers across the usable sessions

Language.value: not explicitly reported; study conducted in the Netherlands and English-language examples/report are provided

Sensitive-data status.value: human-participant audio and transcripts from an on-road study

Model family.value: Google Gemini, xAI Grok, and OpenAI ChatGPT

Exact model/version.value: primary: Gemini 3.0 Pro Preview; robustness: Gemini 2.5 Pro, SuperGrok Expert, and ChatGPT 5 Thinking, each identified with September 2025 availability where stated

Prompting strategy.value: single reproduced prompt asking for recurring themes about human requirements during transitions of control and diverse supporting quotations from all eight transcripts

Human role.value: Researchers designed and ran the study, cleaned transcripts, checked/corrected every LLM-selected quotation against recordings, and interpreted outputs; no independent human coding or theme adjudication was reported.

Unit of analysis.value: complete participant think-aloud transcript and cited utterance

Generated outputs.value: five themes and selected illustrative quotations

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: selected quotations were manually traced to and corrected against source recordings

Baselines.value: same prompt run with Gemini 2.5 Pro, SuperGrok Expert, and ChatGPT 5 Thinking for a qualitative robustness comparison

Number of runs or seeds.value: one reported run per model; seeds and decoding settings not reported

Human-evaluation design.value: quote-level verification only; no independent theme-level human evaluation

Principal results.value: The LLM produced five requirements themes: immediate environmental assessment, causal understanding, proactive intervention, continuous supervisory engagement, and physical ergonomics/mode awareness. Alternative models were said to recover similar content with different granularity, without a formal comparison rubric.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: TU/e ethics approval ERB2024ID465, participant consent, and post-study debriefing are reported.

Author-reported limitations.value: Small homogeneous expert sample, Wizard-of-Oz artificiality, think-aloud reactivity, inconsistent experimental conditions/experimenters, short exposure, and limited transfer to ordinary drivers.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: the LLM alone generated the themes; manual checking verifies quotations but not the thematic interpretation. The cross-model comparison is narrative, unscored, and apparently based on one run per model, while the prompt itself fixes the analytic target.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Useful negative-control case showing why source-verified quotations and cross-model convergence should not be conflated with independent validation of a thematic structure.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed Risk Analysis 2026;46(8):e70324, published online 4 August 2026
records.decision_reason: The paper combines highly validated LLM screening and structured extraction with an LLM-open-code plus researcher-led inductive thematic synthesis; the latter audit is described but not quantified in the main article.

Research objective.value: Map how news media portray evolving human and AI roles in risk analysis and identify paired governance problems and solutions.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: sequential computational and inductive thematic analysis

Actual operationalized methodology.value: A risk dictionary reduced 184,282 Factiva AI-news records, Qwen3.5-27b screened relevance, and the same model extracted domain and role variables. Structural topic modeling analyzed the retained corpus. Qwen then open-coded problem/solution phrases from all retained articles, after which researchers consolidated phrases into codes, subthemes, themes, and a problem-solution mirror map using Braun and Clarke-inspired analysis.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: hybrid: structured screening/extraction and inductive open coding/thematic synthesis

Domain.value: risk analysis, human-AI teaming, and governance in news media

Public or restricted data.value: restricted commercial news data; underlying articles cannot be redistributed

Number of documents.value: 184,282 initial Factiva articles; 16,205 dictionary-filtered; 3,571 retained after LLM screening

Number of participants.value: three human coders for screening validation and a three-researcher qualitative synthesis team; no recruited research participants

Sensitive-data status.value: commercial news archive; no recruited human-subject data

Prompting strategy.value: zero-temperature screening, structured variable extraction, and article-level open-code/problem-solution phrase generation; full prompts are reported in supporting information

Human role.value: Three coders validated screening/extraction reference samples; researchers audited sampled open-code outputs, consolidated thousands of phrases, labeled topic-model outputs, and constructed the final thematic hierarchy and mirror map.

Unit of analysis.value: news article for screening/extraction and article-derived problem/solution phrase for thematic synthesis

Generated outputs.value: relevance labels, domain/human-role/AI-role variables, 20 structural topics, open codes, 30 codes, 15 subthemes, five themes, and five problem-solution mirror pairs

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: article-level extraction; sampled outputs audited and adjudicated by researchers, with prompts in supporting information

Baselines.value: human consensus reference samples for screening and structured extraction; no independent human thematic baseline

Number of runs or seeds.value: single Qwen configuration at temperature 0; STM seed 42; repeated LLM runs not reported

Automatic metrics.value: accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1, Cohen's kappa, prevalence-adjusted predictive values, Fleiss' kappa, and topic-model diagnostics

Human-evaluation design.value: Balanced n=300 screening sample independently coded by three humans; separate n=300 structured-extraction validation; sampled article-level open-code outputs were audited with consensus adjudication, but that audit's n and results are not quantified in the main article.

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: three independent coders for reported validation; qualitative synthesis by three researchers; detailed discipline-specific expertise not reported

Inter-rater reliability.value: screening Fleiss kappa 0.976; structured-variable Fleiss kappas 0.975, 0.969, and 0.980

Principal results.value: Screening reached 96.3% accuracy, 94.7% precision, 97.9% recall, F1 96.3%, and Cohen kappa 0.927. Variable extraction reached 95.0-96.0% exact agreement and kappas 0.925-0.952. The thematic analysis produced paired themes of opacity/explainability, bias/auditing, agency erosion/cognitive friction, systemic fragility/oversight and liability, and accountability vacuums/institutional governance.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Use of licensed news data and redistribution restriction are disclosed; no recruited human-subject data are reported.

Reproducibility resources.value: prompts and additional details are in supporting information; source articles are unavailable for redistribution because of Factiva licensing

Author-reported limitations.value: News coverage is not direct evidence of practice; English/Factiva selection bias; model, prompt, and version dependence; and identified governance mechanisms are not implementation evidence.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: excellent screening and structured-extraction validation does not establish validity of the open-code-to-theme interpretation. The main article omits the sample size and outcomes for its thematic audit, uses one model at one zero-temperature configuration, and assigns single primary categories that may suppress compound meanings.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: A high-value contrast between well-validated objective filtering/extraction and under-quantified interpretive synthesis, motivating stage-specific validity claims.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction 33(1), article 111, published 25 February 2026; DOI 10.1145/3778354; arXiv family 2405.05758v2
records.decision_reason: CHALET is a central hybrid human-LLM qualitative method: it uses prompt-tested deductive coding, systematic disagreement analysis, and collaborative inductive code/theme construction, with both held-out agreement checks and an autonomous-LLM comparison.

Research objective.value: Develop and demonstrate CHALET, a human-LLM framework that treats deductive-coding disagreements as prompts for collaborative inductive theory refinement.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: theory-driven hybrid deductive-inductive qualitative coding with human-LLM collaboration

Actual operationalized methodology.value: A chatbot elicited seven stigma-attribution messages from each participant. Three researchers developed and applied an eight-code attribution-model codebook, compared 23 GPT-4 prompt variants against 4,153 usable human-coded messages, audited cases where all variants disagreed, and collaboratively open-coded the 181 potential-new-code cases using human memos, LLM naming/grouping suggestions, specialist review, consensus, held-out reliability testing, and an autonomous-LLM comparator.

Domain.value: mental-illness stigma and HCI qualitative methodology

Public or restricted data.value: participant-message release status not reported; codebook evolution, prompts, and affinity-diagram materials are reported as supplementary

Number of documents.value: 7,014 participant messages; 4,200 messages selected for human coding, of which 4,153 were usable; 273 all-prompt disagreement cases and 181 potential-new-code cases

Number of participants.value: 1,002 participants; three qualitative coders and one mental-health specialist, with psychiatrist review of elicitation materials

Approximate corpus size.value: seven messages per participant; mean message length about 39-44 words depending on attribution

Language.value: English; first-language English was an inclusion criterion
Language.anchor: speak English as their first language

Sensitive-data status.value: confidential participant conversations about mental illness and stigma

Prompting strategy.value: 23 systematically varied role, codebook-component, example-order, reasoning, and target-code/all-code prompt configurations; temperatures 1, 0.5, and 0 and five-output majority voting were tested. The selected configuration used temperature 0, a competent-coder role, instructions before content, reasoning output, and no majority vote.

Single-agent or multi-agent.value: single LLM collaborating with a multi-person human team

Human role.value: Humans authored and versioned the deductive codebook, independently coded and reconciled labels, audited every selected human-LLM disagreement, generated initial inductive codes and memos, accepted/revised/rejected LLM suggestions, built affinity diagrams, reached consensus, and evaluated the collaborative and LLM-only codebooks.

Unit of analysis.value: individual participant message tied to one attribution question

Generated outputs.value: deductive stigma labels and rationales, disagreement categories, 12 new subthemes and eight codes organized under cognitive, emotional, and behavioral themes, and an expanded codebook

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: participant IDs and excerpts support themes; independent human memos and shared affinity diagrams are linked through supplementary materials

Baselines.value: human-human agreement, 23 prompt configurations, original versus expanded codebooks, and a three-prompt autonomous GPT-4 inductive-coding pipeline

Number of runs or seeds.value: five-output majority voting was tested, but the selected deductive configuration used one temperature-0 output; run counts for inductive suggestions are not reported

Automatic metrics.value: Cohen's kappa, chi-square test for prompt example-order effects, disagreement frequencies, duplicate-code rate, and Likert codebook-quality ratings

Human-evaluation design.value: Three experienced research-team coders performed iterative independent coding and consensus. Three coders plus a mental-health specialist rated collaborative and autonomous-LLM codebooks on clarity, mutual exclusivity, ease of use, and exhaustiveness. A fresh 100-message sample from the remaining 402 participants tested original versus expanded codebook agreement.

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: three qualitative coders (two computer science, one social science, all with prior qualitative-coding experience), plus a mental-health specialist; a psychiatrist reviewed data-collection materials

Inter-rater reliability.value: overall human-human kappa 0.71, recheck kappa 0.69; best human-LLM kappa 0.69; human review on previously uncoded messages kappa 0.87; fresh-sample human-human kappa improved from 0.67 to 0.87 with the expanded scheme

Statistical analysis.value: Cohen's kappa with 95% confidence intervals for prompt conditions; example-order primacy chi-square chi2(4,N=4,153)=85.04, p<.001

Principal results.value: Full codebook context raised human-LLM kappa from 0.60 to 0.75 in a cited comparison and rules raised it from 0.30 to 0.58. Of 273 unanimous prompt disagreements, 51 were human errors, 41 LLM errors, and 181 suggested new codes. Collaborative coding produced 12 new subthemes and eight codes; the expanded scheme raised all-message human-LLM kappa from 0.69 to 0.72 and fresh-sample human-human kappa from 0.67 to 0.87. Experts rated the collaborative codebook above the autonomous one on all four criteria; 61.54% of autonomous codes were duplicates.

Efficiency or cost results.value: participants received about US$6.30 for a 30-minute study; computational cost and human coding time are not quantified

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Consent, confidentiality, withdrawal rights, a mental-health distress exclusion, omission of extreme vignette symptoms, warning, and debriefing are described; institutional ethics-board approval/identifier is not reported in the inspected article.

Reproducibility resources.value: supplementary materials contain prompt templates/configurations, versioned codebooks, and affinity diagrams; participant-message and executable-code availability are not reported

Author-reported limitations.value: Single case and single GPT-4 model; possible LLM/Western cultural bias; nonrepresentative Western participant pool; human-chatbot interactions omit nonverbal cues and differ from human interviews; message-level analysis misses conversation trajectories.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: prompt selection and evaluation use the same 4,153 human-coded messages, so the main 0.69 agreement is not held out; only 100 fresh messages assess codebook generalization. The conservative all-23-prompts disagreement filter conditions inductive discovery on unusual cases, and consensus with an involved specialist is not an independent test of theoretical truth. Ethics-board approval is not reported despite sensitive recruited-participant data.

Relationship to prior papers.value: Preferred peer-reviewed version of arXiv:2405.05758 and the earlier OpenReview title represented by TA-1299.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Directly advances disagreement-as-discovery and human-governed inductive refinement, while exposing design needs for nested holdouts, provenance of LLM suggestions, and separation of agreement from interpretive validity.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed ECIR 2026 proceedings chapter in Advances in Information Retrieval, LNCS, pages 139-154; DOI 10.1007/978-3-032-21300-6_9; arXiv 2601.15338v1
records.decision_reason: The paper directly operationalizes LLM open and axial coding and benchmarks clustering-based versus direct LLM category induction, but uses administrative topic-taxonomy similarity rather than human qualitative judgment of the induced categories.

Research objective.value: Operationalize scalable axial coding of political debates by grouping ensemble-generated open codes into higher-order categories and compare clustering with direct LLM grouping.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: automated open and axial qualitative coding

Actual operationalized methodology.value: LoRA-adapted instruction models propose one open code per utterance, an LLM moderator chooses/refines it, and SBERT similarity consolidates labels. Axial categories are then induced either by embedding code-utterance pairs and clustering them or by asking three LLMs to group 200-500 items per batch; category labels and memberships are merged by cosine/Jaccard thresholds and evaluated against an administrative topic taxonomy plus intrinsic clustering metrics.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: inductive code/category generation, evaluated against deductive human-curated topic labels

Domain.value: Dutch parliamentary debates and political information retrieval

Dataset name.value: Dutch parliamentary debate transcripts with government domain/subtopic metadata

Public or restricted data.value: 5,000-utterance test subset and generated codes/categories publicly released

Number of documents.value: 2,038 debates in the full corpus; 578 train debates and 196 held-out test debates

Number of participants.value: 248 speakers in the full corpus; no human qualitative evaluators

Approximate corpus size.value: 82,732 utterances full corpus; 20,000 train utterances and 5,000 held-out test utterances

Document length.value: full corpus mean/max 4,844/124,352 words per debate; test mean/max 3,178/50,129

Language.value: Dutch debate source; whether preprocessing or translation to model input language occurred is not reported

Model family.value: LLaMA-3, Falcon, Mistral open-code ensemble; DeepSeek, Llama, and Mixtral axial grouping; SBERT-family encoders

Exact model/version.value: axial grouping: Deepseek-R1, Llama-4 Maverick, Mixtral 8x7B; open-code candidate and moderator checkpoints are not exactly specified in this paper

Prompting strategy.value: candidate open-code prompts request 1-5-word abstractions; moderator selects/refines candidates; direct axial prompts group 200-500 code-utterance pairs into JSON categories of at most five words

Fine-tuning or adaptation.value: LoRA adaptation of open-code candidate models on 1,000 social-science quote-code pairs plus SemEval-2014 Task 4; exact checkpoints/hyperparameters are deferred to prior work

Single-agent or multi-agent.value: multi-model ensemble plus moderator for open coding; three independent LLMs for direct axial grouping

Agent roles.value: candidate open coders, lead-coder moderator, axial groupers, and LLM category labeler after clustering

Human role.value: Government-assigned document topic labels provide an external reference; researchers design metrics and thresholds. No human qualitative coder reviews the generated open codes or axial categories.

Unit of analysis.value: parliamentary utterance paired with one generated open code

Generated outputs.value: one refined open code per utterance, higher-order category assignments and labels, and an illustrative concept graph

Evidence/provenance mechanism.anchor: full dataset of utterances and codes

Baselines.value: DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, KMeans, agglomerative, spectral, and GMM clustering across multiple embeddings, compared with three direct LLM grouping models and human-curated domain/subtopic labels

Number of runs or seeds.value: not reported for LLM generation or clustering sweeps

Automatic metrics.value: silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz, coverage, brevity, coherence, novelty, Jensen-Shannon divergence, ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and BERTScore F1

Human-evaluation design.value: none for generated qualitative codes/categories; the reference is an existing government taxonomy assigned at document level

Principal results.value: HDBSCAN BGE+UMAP covered 96% but collapsed the test set to three categories and reached subtopic ROUGE-L 0.111/cosine 0.300/BERTScore 0.867. Deepseek-R1 had strongest direct-LLM subtopic ROUGE-L 0.248 and cosine 0.328 but only 20.3% coverage. Llama-4 covered 32.8% with weighted coherence 0.576.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: No dedicated ethics statement; data are public parliamentary records

Reproducibility resources.value: GitHub releases the 5,000-item test subset with human labels, open codes, and axial categories; prompts and exact open-coder/moderator checkpoints are incomplete in this paper

Author-reported limitations.value: Single political debate corpus; fixed model/algorithm set; dependence on a clean taxonomy; experiments limited to first-level axial coding rather than deeper hierarchies.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: lexical/embedding similarity to a document-level administrative topic taxonomy is not a validity test of inductive qualitative interpretation. Exact open-code and moderator checkpoints, run counts, seeds, decoding settings, and Dutch-language handling are missing, while cluster-selection metrics favor high-coherence low-coverage solutions.

Relationship to prior papers.value: Extends Parfenova and Pfeffer's ensemble open-coding method with an axial-coding stage.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Adds axial hierarchy, abstention/coverage tradeoffs, and provenance-graph outputs to the evaluation agenda; motivates human assessment distinct from taxonomy-label similarity.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: arXiv preprint 2601.13317v2, revised 24 June 2026; ACL ARR May 2026 submission, with acceptance/peer review not established by the cutoff
records.decision_reason: The paper develops an LLM-labeled thematic discovery and assignment pipeline, compares topic-model baselines, and conducts a substantial seven-researcher evaluation, while stopping short of expert interpretive validation of the cross-platform substantive themes.

Research objective.value: Develop and validate an interpretable, seed-free thematic discovery pipeline and use it to compare paid Meta climate advertising with organic Bluesky climate discourse.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: interpretable cross-platform thematic analysis combining quantitative and qualitative analysis

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Climate-keyword retrieval and SBERT deduplication yielded 17,026 Meta ads and 19,182 sampled Bluesky posts. Per platform, SBERT/PCA/UMAP/HDBSCAN formed clusters; Mistral filtered coherence, summarized top-five representatives, merged clusters, labeled themes, and assigned each text by summary or label. Seven researchers judged 500 items per platform against LDA, BERTopic, TopicGPT, and the two proposed assignments; joint clustering then supported prevalence, framing, register, stance, temporal, and retrieval analyses.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: hybrid: seed-free inductive theme discovery followed by fixed-theme assignment and deductive framing/stance analyses

Domain.value: climate communication, paid political advertising, and social-media discourse

Dataset name.value: Paid Voices vs. Public Feeds Meta Ad Library and Bluesky climate corpus

Public or restricted data.value: datasets and code publicly released on GitHub, subject to platform/content constraints

Number of documents.value: 113,493 collected Meta ads reduced to 17,026; about 1.3 million collected Bluesky posts, with 20,000 sampled and 19,182 retained; 36,206 texts in joint analysis

Number of participants.value: seven human evaluators; social-media authors/advertisers were not recruited and unique-user count is not reported

Approximate corpus size.value: 36,208 per-platform analytic texts (17,026 Meta plus 19,182 Bluesky); 36,206 stated for joint clustering

Language.value: not explicitly reported; English-language keywords, prompts, examples, and models indicate an English-focused corpus

Sensitive-data status.value: public social-media posts and political advertisements that may contain offensive, biased, toxic, or harmful language

Model family.value: Mistral Large for thematic pipeline; Qwen3 LLM judge; Llama 3.1 and Kimi K2 downstream

Exact model/version.value: Mistral-Large-Instruct-2407; Qwen3-235b-a22b; llama-3.1-8b-instant; moonshotai/kimi-k2-instruct-0905; exact TopicGPT generator checkpoint not reported

Prompting strategy.value: few-shot cluster-coherence classification, top-five-representative summarization, 1-3-word theme labeling, and batch-of-ten text-to-summary/text-to-theme assignment; prompts are reproduced in the appendix

Single-agent or multi-agent.value: single-model staged thematic pipeline plus a separate LLM judge

Human role.value: Researchers selected data/thresholds and interpreted platform patterns; seven NLP/CSS researchers judged assignment correctness and a smaller retrieval sample. Humans did not independently construct or adjudicate the discovered theme inventory.

Unit of analysis.value: individual advertisement or Bluesky post; cluster/theme for higher-level comparisons

Generated outputs.value: 47 Meta themes, 46 Bluesky themes, 354 coherent joint themes, per-text assignments, platform-dominance categories, framing/register measures, stance predictions, and retrieval rankings

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: each cluster summary/theme is grounded in its top five highest-probability texts; code/data release supports text-to-theme traceability

Baselines.value: LDA, BERTopic, TopicGPT, text-to-summary versus text-to-theme assignment, human versus Qwen judging, and downstream text-only/theme-only/combined stance models

Number of runs or seeds.value: main LLM-generation runs and decoding settings not reported; downstream splits use a fixed but unreported random seed

Automatic metrics.value: silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, accuracy, raw agreement, Cohen's kappa, pairwise cosine redundancy, stance accuracy/macro-F1, precision@1/5, rank-biserial correlations, and statistical tests for temporal/register comparisons

Human-evaluation design.value: Seven NLP/CSS researchers completed three roughly 1.5-hour sessions judging theme/keyword correctness on random samples of 500 Meta ads and 500 Bluesky posts using the LLM judge instructions; a separate random 20 themes x top-five retrieval assessment per platform used a 0-2 relevance rubric.

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: seven NLP and computational-social-science researchers: advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and faculty; ages 20-40, three men and four women

Inter-rater reliability.value: human-versus-Qwen agreement: Meta summary 79.23%, kappa 0.58; Meta theme 77.42%, kappa 0.50; Bluesky summary 71.4%, kappa 0.44; Bluesky theme 70.4%, kappa 0.40; TopicGPT 90.2%, kappa 0.43. Human-human item overlap/reliability is not reported.

Principal results.value: Human accuracy for the proposed text-to-theme assignment was 0.67 on both platforms, above LDA/BERTopic but below broad TopicGPT labels (0.95 Meta, 0.93 Bluesky). Meta and Bluesky pipelines yielded 47 and 46 themes; joint analysis produced 145 Meta-dominant, 112 Bluesky-dominant, and 97 shared themes. Theme-guided human P@5 was 0.60 Meta and 0.73 Bluesky, and themes added stance-prediction signal, especially on Meta.

Efficiency or cost results.value: Human annotation took about 11 hours total; model-compute cost for the thematic pipeline is not reported

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Authors state compliance with ethical norms, warn that public posts may contain harmful language, disclose academic-only LIWC licensing, anonymize/paraphrase illustrative content, and release data/code; consent and a formal ethics review are not reported for public-platform data.

Reproducibility resources.value: GitHub repository releases datasets and code; appendices reproduce prompts and most processing thresholds/model versions

Author-reported limitations.value: Only two structurally confounded platforms; unavailable comparable demographics; model/prompt and climate-calibrated threshold dependence; unmeasured LLM bias; no fine-tuning; descriptive rather than causal conclusions.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: human evaluation tests whether fixed assignments fit individual texts, not whether the LLM-discovered theme inventory is interpretively complete, nonredundant, or useful for the substantive cross-platform claims. Human-human overlap/reliability and main generation runs/seeds are unreported; treating Meta as institutional and Bluesky as organic leaves major platform/user/time confounds; the per-platform total differs by two from the joint-analysis denominator.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Strong benchmark for theme-inventory and assignment evaluation, source grounding, downstream utility, and platform-shift auditing; also motivates explicit interpretive-inventory review separate from item-fit judgments.
